text: Caldwell Logistics' order-tracking app stores invoice PDFs in an Azure Storage account and reads order data from an Azure SQL database. The storage account is already encrypted at rest with Microsoft-managed keys by default, but the compliance team now wants its own customer-managed key for control over rotation and revocation — and the app's database connection string has been sitting in plain text in a config file since launch, exactly the mistake Lesson 13 warned about.

A customer-managed key has to live in a Key Vault with soft-delete and purge protection both enabled, since Azure needs a guarantee the key can't disappear out from under an encrypted storage account. After creating the vault and the key inside it, the storage account's managed identity needs the Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User role — without it, the account can reference the key but can't actually use it. One more command points the storage account's encryption source at that key.

The fix for the hardcoded connection string is storing it as a Key Vault secret with az keyvault secret set, instead of a literal value in appsettings.json. The app never hardcodes the raw string anywhere — it authenticates with its own managed identity through DefaultAzureCredential and asks a SecretClient for it at startup, or an App Service pulls it in through a Key Vault reference in its app settings. Either way, the real value lives in exactly one place.

That one place beats a hardcoded string on every count from Lesson 13: nothing to leak through Git history because it was never committed, nothing for a build log or container layer to capture, and every single read of the secret shows up in Key Vault's own access log, tied to the identity that requested it.

Rotation works differently for the two. The customer-managed key supports an automatic rotation policy — Key Vault generates a new version on a schedule with no human involved. The connection string can't work that way, because Key Vault has no way to generate a new database password on its own. It can only set an expiration date and fire an Event Grid notification as that date approaches, which Caldwell wires to a small Function that actually rotates the SQL credential and writes the new value back.

Encryption at rest with a key Caldwell controls, and a secret that's actually a secret instead of a line in a config file — both now have a real rotation story behind them. Next up: Lesson 31 walks through a real CSPM finding on that same storage account, how it happened, and how it actually gets fixed.
